value.title: Identity of self
value.summary: Ways to follow children who say "that's me," want their name written, notice who looks like them and tell who is in their family.

sections.text: Children find themselves in every photo and say "that's me." They ask whose cubby, whose name, whose shoes. They want their name written on everything they make and begin to write it themselves. They notice skin, hair, eyes and size, and ask who looks like them. They tell long stories about their family, their pets and their house, and carry a photo people figure of themselves into the blocks, the small world and the puppet theater.

items: Photo people, each child's photograph laminated and stood up with a binder clip, or glued to a block, kept in a basket for stories, building and small worlds.
A name card for each child with their photo, their name and their name in their home language, at the sign-in table and on their cubby.
A Me basket in the class atelier with a hand mirror, the child's photo people figure and paper and pencil for a self-portrait.
Self-portraits at a mirror, offered again and again through the year, with each one dated and kept.
Skin, hair and eye color paints mixed with each child, each color named by the child.
An All About Me book made over weeks, with a photo, a self-portrait, a handprint, favorite things and family words.
Family photos at children's eye level, chosen and sent by families, with the names of everyone in them.
Each child's baby photo beside a photo of them now, with guesses and stories.
A measuring wall where each child's height is marked and dated with their photo beside it.
A class book of "who I am," one page each in the child's own words, kept in the reading nook.
Songs with each child's name, and the class names clapped in beats at meeting time.
A portrait of a friend drawn face to face, then the pair shown together.
Real photos of children and families from many places and cultures at eye level.
Books about names, families, bodies and belonging from the Book collection.

sections.text: Both. A self-portrait at the mirror is quiet personal work. Photo people in the blocks and the class book of names draw children into noticing each other.

Photos of children's faces stay inside our walls and never go online or in public. Ask families before sharing a photo beyond the class. Honor every skin color, feature, name and family shape, and answer questions about differences plainly and warmly. Say each child's name the way their family says it. Keep every self-portrait so children and families can see the year's change.

items: Decide what their photo people figure does and where it goes.
Write or trace their own name.
Mix and name their own colors.
Choose what goes in their All About Me book and what stays private.
Tell who is in their family and in their house.
Help put the family photos and name cards where everyone can see them.

sections.text: Photo people go back in their basket and name cards back on the table or cubby. Mirrors are wiped with the soft cloth. Self-portraits go on the drying rack or into the child's own folder. Photo labels show each thing's home.

Sit beside the child and let them name what they see. Describe without judging looks, such as Your hair curls at the ends. Use the child's name the way their family says it and learn how it is written in their home language. When a child asks why a friend looks different, answer plainly and warmly.

items: Tell me about you.
I wonder who is in your family.
What do you notice about your face today?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with name cards with photos at the sign-in table.
For twos and threes, offer a floor mirror, their photo on their cubby and their name sung at meeting time.
Make photo people with the children and set the basket by the blocks.
Offer self-portraits at a mirror and keep each one dated.
Mix skin, hair and eye color paints with each child.
Invite families to send photos and family words for a wall at eye level.
Start All About Me books, a page at a time.
Add baby photos beside photos now and talk about change.
Learn each child's name in their home language and how it is written.
For fours, fives and TK, write their own page for the class book of who I am.
Return to the self-portraits in spring and set them side by side.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Mirrors, photos and name cards are open to everyone, and paint mixing is an adult at the table.

value.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer pounding and pressing clay into a face, a big floor mirror for whole-body faces, and hard pressing with oil pastels.
value.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a hand mirror and their own photo to look at alone, and a pencil drawing over paint.
connected: The Image of the Child lens

sections.text: A mirror, paper, a pencil and a few family photos.

items: Look in the mirror together and name what you see.
Draw a self-portrait and write the date on it.
Make a photo person of your child with a photo, a piece of card and a clothespin.
Tell the story of your child's name.
Look at baby photos together.

sections.text: Your child chooses what to draw and what to say, and puts the photos away.

items: Tell me about you.
Who is in our family?
What was your name as a baby?

sections.text: Your child is learning that they belong and that who they are is seen and named with care (identity and belonging).
Send a family photo or your child's self-portrait for the family wall. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Keep photos of your child off public pages, and let your child decide what to share.
